claims.text: Atomic-size mismatches among constituent elements produce lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys.
An optimal degree of lattice distortion suppresses enthalpy-driven ordering at low temperatures.
Enthalpy-driven ordering promotes secondary-phase formation at low temperatures.
Suppressing ordering and secondary-phase formation stabilizes a single-phase disordered structure.
The stabilized single-phase structure retains high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni can be prepared in a predominantly single-phase solid-solution state.
Systematically changing Al concentration, or that of another element with a distinct atomic radius, will modify the magnitude of lattice distortion.
A sufficient degree of lattice distortion increases the activation barrier for ordering.
A sufficient degree of lattice distortion increases the activation barrier for forming detrimental secondary phases.
Configurational entropy increasingly stabilizes a solid-solution state at elevated temperatures.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch up to a critical threshold will delay or suppress secondary-phase formation relative to equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.

Increasing atomic-size mismatch up to a critical threshold will improve the combined high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy is the standard baseline composition.
Excessive atomic-size mismatch can create strains large enough to cause brittleness.
Excessive atomic-size mismatch can directly cause precipitation of secondary phases.
The critical lattice-distortion threshold may depend on processing conditions and minor compositional variations.
Failure of increased lattice distortion to suppress secondary phases or improve targeted properties relative to the baseline would falsify lattice distortion as the key mediator.
